pr_title: Bluetooth: Controller: Fix instant based procedure complete event
pr_body:
Fix instant based procedure complete event generation to be
held until after the on-air instant has elapsed.

Fixes #21994.

Signed-off-by: Vinayak Kariappa Chettimada <vich@nordicsemi.no>

review_comments: @erbr-ot Do I need the conditional compilation as non of the CI tests are complaining?
Well, the rx_hold-functionality is under CONFIG_BT_LL_SW_LLCP_LEGACY is it not? So I'd expect the usage to be as well?
I guess no builds are made with refactored LLCP AND CONFIG_BT_CTLR_RX_ENQUEUE_HOLD?
@kruithofa can confirm, the bsim LL conformance tests run the refactored LLCP, but I do not think CONFIG_BT_CTLR_RX_ENQUEUE_HOLD would be enabled?
@erbr-ot I have added the depends on CONFIG_BT_LL_SW_LLCP_LEGACY

I am a bit curious about the value ranges of these variables. They are not limited to the `RX_HOLD_REQ` and `RX_HOLD_ACK` values, right? 

Do they ever exceed 0x0F? In other words, could they both be in a single uint8_t?
Being in single `uint8_t` would not be context-safe as the memory of `rx_hold_req` and `rx_hold_ack`  would both get corrupted when there is context switch in between read-modify-write.

> Oh, so there's a difference between having
> 
> ```c
> uint8_t rx_hold_req : 4;
> uint8_t rx_hold_ack : 4;
> ```
> 

This is not context-safe, will need custom interrupt locking and be not usable with `__atomic` builtin functions. (that said, controller code design is to be lock-less to reduce CPU use and does not use `__atomic` builtin but instead depend on the fact that uint8_t, uint16_t and uint32_t load and store are atomic in ARM cortex-M CPUs)

> 
> ```c
> uint8_t rx_hold_req;
> uint8_t rx_hold_ack;
> ```
> 
> or even using macros to set/get the individual bits in terms of context-safety?

Using macros to set/get need custom interrupt locking as `__atomic` builtin functions can only be used with any integral scalar or pointer type that is 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes in length

Controller design extensively uses bare-metal implementation of double buffers, request and acknowledge, head and tail, first and last variables of 1, 2, or 4 bytes of length between two execution contexts to have a lockless implementation.
Thanks for your response - Was not aware of that :)
Any risk that `rx_last == rx_last->hdr.link->mem` and thus ending in an infinite loop here?

`rx_last->hdr.link->mem` is always assigned the supplied `rx` which is an allocation by the caller of this function.

Once in the `conn->llcp_rx_hold` linked list, only call to `rx_hold_flush()` would lead to the eventual release of `rx` back to pool. Value in each traversal of `rx_last->hdr.link->mem` will be unique reference to an allocated `struct node_rx_pdu *` pointer.

There will not be an infinite loop, unless an external corruption of memory.

> There will not be an infinite loop, unless an external corruption of memory.

So there's no risk of a code bug may introduce an infinite loop, which are notoriously hard to find and debug?

Just wondering if we should insert an __ASSERT that verified that `rx_last != rx_last->hdr.link->mem` before updating the pointer.

A simple check cannot detect an external code corrupting a linked. I do not think it is feasible to detect loops in linked lists. Connecting a debugger to a hung board or watchdog should catch infinite loops.
